Cervical Spine Fractures & Dislocations

Upper Cervical (C0–C2) & Subaxial (C3–C7) Injuries

1.5–3.5%of Major Trauma
C2Most Common Level
15/100KAnnual Incidence
6 SystemsClassification

Epidemiology

  • Cervical spine injuries occur in 1.5–3.5% of major trauma patients
  • Population-adjusted incidence increased by 74% from 1997 to 2006 in the US, with total healthcare costs exceeding $1 billion
  • Annual incidence of cervical fractures: 15 per 100,000 residents (Norwegian registry); 3 per 100,000 undergo surgery
  • Bimodal age distribution: younger patients (high-energy mechanisms) and elderly (falls, osteoporosis)
  • Risk factors: male sex, younger age, low GCS, low systolic BP, severe facial fractures
  • The upper cervical region (C0–C2) is the most frequent fracture site; C2 is the single most commonly fractured vertebra
  • Spinal cord injury incidence: approximately 40 per million in civilian populations

Mechanism of Injury

  • Motor vehicle collisions — most common cause overall; deceleration injuries produce flexion-distraction patterns
  • Falls — increasingly important in elderly; often produce odontoid (Type II) or hangman's fractures
  • Diving/sports — axial loading produces burst-type and compression injuries
  • Penetrating trauma — gunshot wounds; less amenable to rigid classification systems
  • Mechanism influences fracture morphology — Allen and Ferguson described 6 injury groups based on force vector: compressive flexion, vertical compression, distractive flexion, compressive extension, distractive extension, lateral flexion

Clinical Assessment

  • ATLS protocol: primary survey with cervical spine immobilization maintained until clinical and radiographic clearance
  • Awake, alert patients: NEXUS criteria or Canadian C-Spine Rule used to determine need for imaging
  • NEXUS low-risk criteria — imaging can be deferred if ALL of: no posterior midline tenderness, no focal neurologic deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, no distracting injury
  • Canadian C-Spine Rule — high-risk factors (age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, paresthesias) mandate imaging; low-risk factors (simple rear-end MVC, sitting in ED, ambulatory, delayed-onset neck pain, absent midline tenderness) permit assessment of active ROM
  • Neurologic examination: ASIA/ISNCSCI motor and sensory grading (Grades A–E)

Imaging

  • CT scan — modality of choice for trauma evaluation; axial images with sagittal and coronal reformats; superior to plain radiographs for fracture detection
  • MRI — essential for evaluating the discoligamentous complex (DLC), spinal cord injury, epidural hematoma, disc herniation, and vertebral artery injury; STIR sequences detect ligamentous edema
  • Plain radiographs — AP, lateral, open-mouth odontoid views; largely supplanted by CT in trauma settings; lateral film must visualize C7–T1 junction
  • CT angiography (CTA) — indicated when vertebral artery injury is suspected (facet dislocation, transverse foramen fracture, C1–C3 fractures)

Radiographic Measurements

Several key radiographic measurements guide diagnosis of upper cervical instability:

Power's Ratio
BC/OA ratio; >1.0 suggests atlantooccipital dislocation. Limited by inability to detect Type II (distraction) injuries.
Harris Rule of 12
BAI and BDI each <12 mm on radiographs. BDI threshold revised to <8.5 mm on CT. Preferred method per Spine Trauma Study Group.
ADI
Atlanto-dens interval: ≤3 mm adults, ≤5 mm children. >3 mm = transverse ligament disruption.
Rule of Spence
Combined lateral mass overhang of C1 on C2 >6.9 mm (XR) or >8.1 mm (CT) suggests transverse ligament rupture in Jefferson fractures. Recent studies question reliability.

Upper Cervical Spine (C0–C2)

  • Occiput (C0) — occipital condyles articulate with superior facets of C1; tectorial membrane and alar ligaments provide primary stability to the occipitocervical junction
  • Atlas (C1) — ring-shaped vertebra with no vertebral body or spinous process; composed of anterior arch, posterior arch, and two lateral masses; articulates with occipital condyles superiorly and C2 facets inferiorly
  • Axis (C2) — unique odontoid process (dens) projects superiorly from the body; the transverse ligament of the atlas is the primary restraint against anterior translation of C1 on C2
  • Transverse ligament — strongest individual ligament in the upper cervical spine; rupture results in atlantoaxial instability (ADI >3 mm)
  • Alar ligaments — limit axial rotation and lateral bending of C0–C1; connect the dens tip to the occipital condyles
  • C1–C2 articulation accounts for approximately 50% of cervical rotation
  • C0–C1 articulation provides approximately 50% of cervical flexion–extension

Lower Cervical Spine (C3–C7)

Fig 48-19. Subaxial cervical vertebra — the transverse process has two components: the anterior portion (costal remnant) and the posterior portion (true transverse process), forming the transverse foramen.
  • Subaxial vertebrae (C3–C7) share a uniform structure: vertebral body, pedicles, lateral masses, laminae, spinous process
  • Transverse foramen — formed by the costal element (anterior tubercle) and true transverse process (posterior tubercle); transmits the vertebral artery from C6 to C1
  • Uncovertebral joints (joints of Luschka) — saddle-shaped articulations on the posterolateral vertebral body; contribute to lateral bending and protect against posterolateral disc herniation
  • Facet joints — oriented at approximately 45° in the coronal plane; the inclined orientation facilitates flexion-extension but makes the subaxial spine susceptible to translational injuries
  • Posterior ligamentous complex (PLC) — supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, and facet joint capsules; critical posterior tension band
  • Anterior longitudinal ligament (ALL) — resists extension; Posterior longitudinal ligament (PLL) — resists flexion

Cervical Spinal Cord

Fig 48-22. Cross-section of the spinal cord showing somatotopic patterns: central cord, anterior cord, Brown-Séquard, fasciculus gracilis/cuneatus, and lateral spinothalamic tract.
  • Central cord syndrome — most common incomplete SCI pattern; upper extremity weakness greater than lower extremity; caused by hyperextension injuries in patients with pre-existing stenosis; somatotopic arrangement places cervical fibres centrally
  • Anterior cord syndrome — loss of motor function, pain, and temperature below the level of injury; preservation of posterior column function (proprioception, vibration); worst prognosis for recovery of all incomplete patterns
  • Brown-Séquard syndrome — hemisection of the cord; ipsilateral motor paralysis and loss of proprioception; contralateral loss of pain and temperature; best prognosis for recovery
  • Posterior cord syndrome — rare; loss of proprioception and vibration with preserved motor, pain, and temperature function

ASIA Impairment Scale

Grade A
Complete — no motor or sensory function below the level of injury (including S4–S5)
Grade B
Sensory incomplete — sensory but no motor function preserved below the level, including S4–S5
Grade C
Motor incomplete — motor function preserved below the level; majority of key muscles <3/5
Grade D
Motor incomplete — motor function preserved below the level; majority of key muscles ≥3/5
Grade E
Normal — motor and sensory function intact

Vertebral Artery

  • Enters the transverse foramen at C6 (most commonly), ascends through C5–C1 foramina
  • Tortuous course around the C1 lateral mass — at risk during C1–C2 screw fixation and posterior arch exposure
  • Dominant artery (usually left) may be the sole supply to the posterior circulation in some patients
  • Risk of vertebral artery injury with: transverse foramen fractures, facet dislocations (especially C3–C7), C1–C2 transarticular screws

Odontoid Fractures — Anderson & D'Alonzo

Fig 48-40. Levine-Edwards: Type I = minimal displacement, Type Ia = atypical posterior body fragment, Type II = angulation + translation, Type IIa = angulation only (do NOT traction), Type III = with facet dislocation.

Fig 48-44. Distractive flexion: facet subluxation → unilateral → bilateral dislocation → complete translation.

SLIC Scoring System

The Subaxial Cervical Spine Injury Classification (SLIC) system scores injuries across three categories to guide treatment decisions.

CategoryParameterPoints
MorphologyNo abnormality0
Compression1
Burst+1
Distraction3
Rotation / Translation4
DLC StatusIntact0
Indeterminate1
Disrupted2
Neurologic StatusIntact0
Root injury1
Complete cord injury2
Incomplete cord injury3
+ Ongoing cord compression+1
SLIC Treatment Algorithm: Score ≤3 → nonoperative; Score ≥5 → surgical; Score = 4 → surgeon discretion based on patient factors (comorbidities, concomitant injuries, neurologic status). Surgeons agreed with the SLIC treatment recommendation in 93% of cases.

General Principles

  • Nonoperative indications: stable fracture patterns, no neurologic deficits, comorbidities precluding surgery
  • Operative indications: mechanical instability, neurologic deficits with canal compromise, progressive neurologic deterioration, failure of nonoperative treatment, symptomatic nonunion
  • Cervical orthoses (soft collar, rigid collar, CTO) restrict but do not eliminate motion — they serve primarily as a reminder to limit activity
  • Miami J collar is popular due to rigidity comparable to CTO for upper cervical immobilization

Upper Cervical Injuries

Occipitocervical Dislocation (C0–C1)

  • These injuries represent internal decapitation — historically almost universally fatal; survivors are increasingly identified with improved prehospital care
  • Delayed diagnosis is common (average 2-day delay in one series); secondary neurologic decline occurred in 29%
  • Treatment: immediate immobilization; avoid traction (risk of further distraction); definitive treatment is occipitocervical fusion
  • Nonoperative management (halo) has unacceptable failure rates and is not recommended

Occipital Condyle Fractures

Nonoperative

  • Type I (impaction) — rigid cervical collar
  • Type II (basilar skull extension) — rigid cervical collar
  • Stable Type III — cervical collar or halo

Operative

  • Type III with evidence of craniocervical instability → occipitocervical fusion
  • Associated cranial nerve palsies (hypoglossal, vagus) are documented
  • CTA recommended for Type III injuries (risk of internal carotid dissection)

Atlas Fractures (C1)

  • Jefferson fracture — burst fracture of C1 ring from axial load; bilateral fractures of anterior and posterior arches
  • Combined lateral mass overhang (rule of Spence): >6.9 mm (XR) suggests transverse ligament rupture — recent studies question reliability
  • Intact transverse ligament (ADI ≤3 mm): rigid cervical collar for 8–12 weeks
  • Ruptured transverse ligament (ADI >3 mm): halo vest vs. surgical stabilization (C1–C2 or occipitocervical fusion)

Odontoid Fractures (C2)

Nonoperative

  • Type I: cervical collar — stable avulsion
  • Type II (nondisplaced): hard collar or halo vest; nonunion rates 26–40% with external immobilization
  • Type III: halo vest or rigid collar for 8–12 weeks; healing rates are high due to cancellous bone vascularity

Operative

  • Type II displaced (>5 mm) or angulated (>10°): anterior odontoid screw fixation (preserves rotation) or posterior C1–C2 fusion
  • Elderly patients: higher nonunion rates; consider primary surgical fixation for displaced Type II
  • Posterior C1–C2 fusion options: Gallie, Brooks, Magerl transarticular screws, Harms (C1 lateral mass + C2 pedicle screws)
Risk factors for Type II odontoid nonunion: age >50, displacement >5 mm, angulation >10°, posterior displacement, delayed treatment, smoking. These factors favour surgical fixation.

Hangman's Fractures (C2 Pars)

Nonoperative

  • Type I: rigid cervical collar — stable, ≤3 mm translation
  • Type Ia: cervical collar — high healing rate despite atypical morphology
  • Type II: traction → halo vest immobilization; acceptable alignment maintained in most cases
  • Type IIa: NO traction — reduce with extension/compression via halo apparatus

Operative

  • Type III: surgical stabilization required (facet dislocation)
  • Type II/IIa with failure of closed reduction or neurologic deficit
  • Options: posterior C2–C3 fusion, anterior C2–C3 discectomy and fusion, C2 pars lag screw

Subaxial Cervical Injuries (C3–C7)

Compression Fractures

  • CF Stages 1–2: rigid cervical collar for 6–12 weeks if no posterior ligamentous injury
  • Obtain MRI to assess PLC integrity — STIR signal in interspinous ligaments suggests instability

Burst Fractures (VC Stage 3 / CF Stage 3)

  • Without neurologic deficit and intact PLC: halo vest or rigid collar
  • With neurologic deficit or PLC disruption: anterior corpectomy with strut graft and plate ± supplemental posterior fixation
  • Multilevel corpectomies with anterior-only fixation have high failure rates — posterior supplementation recommended

Facet Injuries

  • Unilateral facet dislocation (DF Stage 2): attempt closed reduction with awake, cooperative patient under fluoroscopy; if irreducible, consider MRI to assess for disc herniation before open reduction
  • Bilateral facet dislocation (DF Stage 3–4): highly unstable; closed reduction followed by operative stabilization (anterior, posterior, or combined approach)
  • Controversy: obtain MRI before vs. after closed reduction for facet dislocations — MRI-first approach delays reduction but identifies disc herniations that could cause cord compression during reduction
  • Anterior plate fixation: less pain, decreased wound infection, increased fusion rates vs. posterior in some studies

Flexion-Teardrop Fractures (CF Stage 3)

  • Highly unstable — the oblique fracture line extends from anterior VB to inferior endplate
  • Typically treated with anterior corpectomy and reconstruction ± posterior stabilization
  • High association with spinal cord injury

Anterior Cervical Approach

Smith-Robinson Approach (Subaxial C3–T1)

  • Position: supine, neck extended; arm tucked, shoulder traction if needed for lower levels
  • Incision: transverse skin crease incision; side of approach is surgeon preference (right-sided approach traditionally favoured to protect left recurrent laryngeal nerve, though studies show no significant difference)
  • Landmarks: hyoid bone = C3, thyroid cartilage = C4–C5, cricoid cartilage/carotid tubercle = C6
  • Interval: between sternocleidomastoid (lateral) and strap muscles (medial); develop plane between carotid sheath (lateral) and oesophagus/trachea (medial)
  • Deep exposure: longus colli muscles identified and retracted laterally to expose disc spaces and vertebral bodies; self-retaining retractors placed under the longus colli
  • Key risks: recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (2–30%), oesophageal perforation, vertebral artery injury (lateral dissection), superior laryngeal nerve (C3–C4 level), sympathetic chain (Horner syndrome)

High Anterior Approach (C1–C3)

  • Submandibular skin incision for access to C1–C3 levels
  • Key structures: submandibular gland, parotid gland, marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve (purely motor — innervates lower lip)
  • Retromandibular vein and common facial vein identified, ligated near internal jugular vein junction
  • Stylohyoid and digastric muscles transected near hyoid insertions, reflected superiorly with hypoglossal nerve
  • Most common complication: marginal mandibular branch facial nerve palsy

Posterior Cervical Approach

Standard Posterior Exposure

  • Position: prone on Jackson table or Mayfield headframe with skull tongs; ensure no pressure on eyes/face
  • Incision: midline from occiput (for occipitocervical) or appropriate spinous process to the desired caudal level
  • Exposure: subperiosteal dissection of paraspinal muscles from spinous processes and laminae; do not extend lateral to the facet joints to preserve the vertebral artery
  • Fluoroscopy used to confirm levels; neuromonitoring (SSEPs/MEPs) recommended if reduction planned

Lateral Mass Screw Fixation (Subaxial)

Fig 48-33. Modified An technique: starting point at superomedial aspect of inferolateral quadrant of the lateral mass. Screw angled 20–25° laterally and kept perpendicular to the facet joint in the sagittal plane.
  • Modified An method (authors' preference): starting hole created with 2-mm burr at the superomedial aspect of the inferolateral quadrant of the lateral mass
  • Trajectory: angled 20–25° laterally in the axial plane; perpendicular to the facet joint plane in the sagittal plane
  • This trajectory places the screw within the midaspect of the lateral mass; unicortical purchase is preferred
  • Screw lengths typically 14–16 mm
  • Key risks: vertebral artery (too medial/deep), nerve root (too inferior/medial), facet joint violation (too cranial)

C1–C2 Fixation Techniques

  • Gallie technique: posterior wiring with structural bone graft; limits rotation but does not resist it — supplemental immobilization often required
  • Brooks technique: bilateral sublaminar wires with wedge grafts; stronger rotational resistance than Gallie
  • Magerl transarticular screws (C1–C2): high fusion rates (95–100%); risk of vertebral artery injury — preoperative CT angiography required to assess anatomy; approximately 20% of patients have anomalous vertebral artery precluding safe screw placement on at least one side
  • Harms technique (C1 lateral mass + C2 pedicle screws): connected by rods; avoids need for C1–C2 reduction prior to screw placement; lower vertebral artery injury risk than Magerl; currently the most popular technique

Occipitocervical Fusion

  • Indicated for occipitocervical dislocations, unstable occipital condyle fractures (Type III), C1 fractures with transverse ligament rupture when C1–C2 fusion alone is insufficient
  • Occipital plate fixed to the midline occipital bone (thickest area: ~15 mm at the external occipital protuberance and midline keel)
  • Construct extended to C2 or beyond depending on caudal extent of injury
  • Significant sacrifice of motion — eliminates ~50% flexion-extension (C0–C1) and ~50% rotation (C1–C2)

Halo Vest Application

  • Anterior pins: 1 cm above the lateral third of the orbital rim — avoids supraorbital nerve
  • Posterior pins: more latitude for placement; ensure ring does not contact the ear
  • Opposing pins tightened simultaneously to avoid ring displacement
  • Final torque: 8 inch-lb; retighten at 24–48 hours
  • Pin complications: loosening and infection in 6–60% of cases

Anterior Approach Complications

  • Dysphagia — most common complication; occurs in up to 50% of cases (subclinical in most); usually transient
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy — presents with dysphonia; incidence 2–30% depending on diagnostic criteria (clinical vs. true vocal cord paralysis); increased risk below C5 and with revision surgery
  • Superior laryngeal nerve injury — rare; dysphagia and loss of high phonation; greatest risk at C3–C4 level
  • Horner syndrome — damage to sympathetic plexus; ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis; infrequent
  • Oesophageal perforation — rare but potentially devastating; requires urgent surgical repair
  • Vertebral artery injury — risk with excessive lateral dissection or decompression; preoperative CTA for anomalous vessels
  • Thoracic duct injury — risk with left-sided approach below C6

Posterior Approach Complications

  • Wound infection — higher rates compared to anterior surgery, particularly with multilevel posterior exposures
  • C5 nerve palsy — motor deficit (deltoid weakness) following posterior decompression; incidence 2–16%; often delayed onset (24–72 hrs); usually recovers over weeks to months
  • Vertebral artery injury — risk with lateral mass screw malposition (too medial/deep), C1–C2 transarticular screws, or excessive lateral dissection beyond the facet joints
  • Durotomy/CSF leak — risk during decompression, especially revision cases or ossified ligamentum flavum
  • Venous thromboembolism — particularly with concomitant spinal cord injury and immobility

Perioperative Neurologic Deficit

  • Risk of neurologic decline during closed reduction of facet dislocations — controversy regarding MRI before vs. after reduction
  • Disc herniation identified in ~50% of facet dislocations on MRI; significance debated
  • Spinal cord monitoring (SSEPs/MEPs) recommended during any reduction manoeuvre or instrumented surgery
  • Overdistraction during traction can worsen neurologic injury — especially dangerous in occult occipitocervical dissociations

Early Postoperative Complications

  • Airway compromise — retropharyngeal haematoma following anterior surgery can cause rapid airway obstruction; requires emergent evacuation
  • Surgical site haematoma — posterior wounds; may require evacuation if causing neurologic compromise
  • Instrumentation malposition — confirmed on postoperative CT; may require revision

Late Postoperative Complications

  • Pseudarthrosis/Nonunion — most common late complication; symptomatic anterior pseudarthrosis can be treated with revision anterior surgery or posterior instrumentation and fusion
  • Hardware failure — screw breakage or plate/graft extrusion; anterior graft or plate extrusion can cause swallowing difficulty, airway compromise, or death
  • Adjacent segment degeneration — radiographic changes in up to 60% of patients by 1 year; clinical significance variable and often not correlated with symptoms
  • Kyphotic deformity — posttraumatic kyphosis from inadequate reduction, graft subsidence, or instrumentation failure; may require revision osteotomy or extension of fusion
  • Multilevel corpectomy failure — anterior-only fixation of ≥2 level corpectomies has a high failure rate; posterior supplementation is recommended

Nonoperative Treatment Complications

  • Halo vest: pin loosening/infection (6–60%), pin-site bleeding, dural penetration (rare), pressure ulcers, dysphagia, restricted pulmonary function, pneumonia (elderly)
  • Cervical collar: pressure ulcers (occiput, mandible angle, sternum), skin maceration, suboptimal immobilization leading to loss of reduction
  • Odontoid nonunion: Type II fractures treated nonoperatively have nonunion rates of 26–40%; elderly patients at highest risk
